en: The characteristic of a mass (piṇḍa) is as follows: 1. A dense mass of color associated with the twins (yamayukta) is like iron;
2. It becomes like a mass, just as gold is within the ore.
The *aghghniyā* [breaths] are for the sake of the body; the *icmīya* [breaths] are for the sake of the beard;

the *parijjman* [breaths] are for the sake of the self; and the *ātman* [breaths] are for the sake of the curd—thus begins the contact with the semi-vowels (*antasthā*). However, a yoga with loose binding is like a block of wood.
5. Sometimes, O Vasus, the *ukthya* sacrifice begins with "The thunderbolt," and so forth.
6. This [type of composition], where the connection between the final aspirated consonant (*oṣman*) and the following letter is loose, is like a tuft of cotton.
7. It is considered "loose connection" (*ślathabandha*) where the letters *ṇa* and *ṇau* are preceded by the letter *va*.
This *ayama* is devoid of the phonetic class of *yama*; it is a mutual connection of the final members of the *ūṣman* series in sequence.
(8) This *ayama* consists of a single cluster (*sakūlapiṇḍa*) and is composed of non-distinctive elements, just as in the case of making known a distinction from a cluster.
(9) For example, among those who discourse on Brahman, at the afternoon of the days, there is a loosening of the bond. (10)
vibhūdāvunne 11, dadhikrāvivīṇṇaḥ 12,
grāvīṇṇaḥ 13.
In the previously mentioned wooden block (*dārupiṇḍa*), the priority of the *sparśa* (stop consonant) was intended;

here, however, the priority of the *vakāra*, which is a semi-vowel (*antasthā*), is intended. This is the distinction regarding the loose articulation (*ślathabandha*). Therefore, this [sound] is not included within the wooden block.
Just as porters bind a load for one who is weary by wrapping it around, so too do they utter the cluster of syllables beginning with *sa-ya-kā-ra*, which is twofold;
this is the *ayantrīṇabandha*. 17–18.
Just as the generative light pervades [it], so do you two, the twin sisters, being in conflict, move apart; here,
in the contact with a stop (sparśa), there is indeed a wooden block in the form of the semi-vowel *ya*.
21. Like the binding of grass with a fiber;
22. This undertaking is for the purpose of knowing the specific [pronunciation] that it should be uttered;
23. The letter *ha* may be either the highest (*uttama*), labial (*oṣṭhya*), nasal (*nāsikya*), or chest-born (*aurasa*).
The *aurasa* [sound] itself follows the semi-vowels (*antasthā*); beyond that is the great resonance (*mahānāda*).
(24) Here, by means of the first half-verse and the fourth statement, he describes the specific distinction within the root-piṇḍa: "Just as...";
"in the autumn, in the afternoon. (25–26)
The *ahannāndīketu* is a specific wooden block mentioned by the third quarter of the verse of the *brahmavādins*;
and according to the statement of Gautama, "by the fourth ṛc, the wooden block is joined with internal stability," here too it is indeed a wooden block. 27–29.
Just as one who eats food satisfies hunger and nourishes the body, so too [the breath] satisfies the [subtle] channels.
By the method of the internal placement of the syllables, having released the wind produced from the nose at the letter *ha*, it should become the air for the subsequent [consonants].

In that case, however, one should pronounce this [letter] separately; since it has been stated that the *ha*-sound is an internal (*antastha*) sound, it should not be abandoned at the region of the throat when preceding these [other sounds],
but rather the *ha*-sound should be pronounced from the chest alone— this is the meaning.
And so says the Śikṣā:
"One should know that the letter *ha* joined with the fifth [sibilants] and combined with the semivowels (*antasthā*) ends in the chest; they say it is guttural when uncombined. (Śikṣā 33–34)
When the letter *ha* follows, one should pronounce it joined with the semivowels (*antasthā*) in their regular order, along with the vowels *i*, *u*, and *ṛ*.
For example, in the case of the Caturhotṛ formulas: "malyahā pratyandīhotāraṃ etān homān.
This [mantra] is also incomplete within the Mātṛkā.
